Building Worlds
In The Beginning
So, you want to build a world?!
Building a brand spanking new world from scratch can be a daunting task. Where do you
even begin? There is a simple answer to that question, which we will repeatedly come
back to throughout this document: the answer is character.
As with all the stories the linchpin that your world revolves around is character. You are not
building a world to play God. You are building a world to help you tell a story, and your
story is all about your characters.
World building involves the creation of an immersive fictional universe that serves as the
backdrop for the film's story. Effective world building enhances the viewer's experience and
engagement with the story, making them believe in and care about the characters and
events within the film. This document explores the art of world building and provides
insights into the key elements and techniques involved, and how you might utilise them to
start building a world of your own.
3

The Shoulder Of Orion
Why is World Building Important?
Distance:
By removing the audience from our world and placing them into a new world, you can
examine topics that might otherwise be too close to home. You can look at societal issues
at arms length and challenge the audience in ways that you may not be able to do
otherwise.
Immersion:
A well-developed, detailed world pulls the audience into the story, making their experience
richer and more enjoyable.
Cohesion:
A carefully constructed world provides a consistent and logical framework for the narrative,
preventing plot holes and inconsistencies, whilst further immersing your audience.
Character Development:
An immersive, cohesive world adds depth to your characters. The world can influence
character backgrounds, motivations, and conflicts, and just as importantly, if not more
importantly, the characters influence the world they inhabit.
World building is a crucial aspect of filmmaking, especially in genres like science fiction

importantly, the characters influence the world they inhabit.
World building is a crucial aspect of filmmaking, especially in genres like science fiction
and fantasy, but there are elements of world building in most, if not all fictional works. You
could be building a Galaxy and every star and planet inside it, or you could be building a
corrupt police department in downtown Boston with just Mark Wahlberg inside it: both are
world building!
There are in essence four types of worlds you can build:
New Worlds:
Completely new worlds with little to no connection with the real world:
Middle Earth, Westeros.
Parallel Words:
A world different to ours, but exists alongside ours:
The Wizarding World of Harry Potter, The Chronicles of Narnia, Space Jam!
Alternative Worlds (alternative history):
Our world in all but name, where a different chain of events have lead to a very different
world:
The Marvel Cinematic Universe, Inglourious Basterds, District 9.
Our World:

Our world in all but name, where a different chain of events have lead to a very different
world:
The Marvel Cinematic Universe, Inglourious Basterds, District 9.
Our World:
Just our world! You don’t always need ray-guns, elves and Quidditch to build a world! If
you are writing about a fictional cowboy, in a non fictional town, in the wild wild west, you
are still building their world. (Although having said that, I would definitely buy a ticket to
watch cowboys with ray-guns play elves at Quidditch!)
Once you understand the type of world you are going to build, there are two questions you
need to ask yourself:
4

What is my genre?
We often do not give too much thought to what genre we are writing because we tend to
instinctively know it. Obviously Star Wars is Sci-Fi, Lord of the Rings is fantasy, and
Ironman is Superhero. But having a clear knowledge of what genre you are writing about
allows you to lean on genre specific troupes that can often get you out of tight corners
whilst writing. Having this clear knowledge also allows to you cross genres, both Star Wars
and Lord of the Rings are war films, both are coming of age stories. Knowing this will give
you a structural blueprint and the clarity you need to help shape your story and build your
world.
Who is my target audience?
It seems obvious, but knowing the demographic you are writing for is crucial. It dictates the
language, tone and content of your story as well as being how you market the thing.
Whether you are writing for children or adults, liberal or conservatives, boys or girls, this

language, tone and content of your story as well as being how you market the thing.
Whether you are writing for children or adults, liberal or conservatives, boys or girls, this
can have a large effect on every aspect of your story, and therefore every aspect of your
world. This should be measured carefully before laying the first brick.
5

Iceberg Right Ahead!
Sanderson:
(Here’s a good moment to mention Brandon Sanderson (author of many works, including
the Mistborn Trilogy and the Stormlight Archive). He gave a series of lectures at Brigham
Young University on writing Science Fiction and Fantasy. He made these lectures available
for free on Youtube and they are an invaluable resource for any writer, whether you work in
prose or film, or in Sci-Fi Fantasy or not. These lectures colour much of next couple of
sections and I would strongly advise all writers of any level of ability and experience to give
them a watch.)
The Hollow Iceberg Theory:
“I always try to write on the principle of the iceberg. There is seven-eighths of it underwater
for every part that shows. Anything you know, you can eliminate and it only strengthens
your iceberg.” — Ernest Hemingway
“Hemingway said that only the tip of the iceberg showed in fiction—your reader will see

your iceberg.” — Ernest Hemingway
“Hemingway said that only the tip of the iceberg showed in fiction—your reader will see
only what is above the water—but the knowledge that you have about your character that
never makes it into the story acts as the bulk of the iceberg. And that is what gives your
story weight and gravitas.” — Jenna Blum
Hemingway is right, but he is also wrong! Sanderson accepts the importance of
Hemingway’s Iceberg Theory but points out that, yes, the audience can only see the tip of
the iceberg and, yes, when they look into the water they need to have the impression of
the full iceberg below, but that iceberg can be hollow.
You do not need to work out every single minute detail of your world. You need to work out
what is important to the story and what is important for you to you to write the story. The
audience need to feel the depth of your world but they will never see beyond the tip of the

what is important to the story and what is important for you to you to write the story. The
audience need to feel the depth of your world but they will never see beyond the tip of the
iceberg. Just do as much as you need for you to tell your story as effectively as possible.
We are not all J.R.R. Tolkien or George R.R. Martin. We can’t all spend the better chunk of
our lives developing an entire world, its complete history, and every language ever spoken
in it. Of course if this is what interests you then by all means do it, but do not feel obliged
to. You are building a world to tell a story, not to live in it.
6

Don’t Panic!
The Eye of the Beholder:
Some artists do hyper detailed paintings with a million intricate strokes. Some paint a
canvas a single colour and sell it for millions. Both are art. There is an audience for both. If
you are feeling overwhelmed by the detail, then don’t focus on the details. There’s no one
way to tell a story or build a world.
Fix it in Post!:
If you’re in any way intimidated about world building, don’t worry about it. Write your story
and then come back to it and fill in the details later.
The Devil’s in the Detail:
Start Simple. It’s easy to get bogged down in the detail. Deliver your world building through
the eyes of the characters. Ground your audience by grounding your characters in the
world. Focus in on something clear that your character wants, and they must proactively
interact with the world to get, and only include details of your world necessary to tell that
journey and nothing more.

interact with the world to get, and only include details of your world necessary to tell that
journey and nothing more.
If you start with a scene that is set in Hogwarts, you have a hell of a lot of explaining to do
to catch the audience up with the inner workings of your world, and this could potentially
alienate the audience. Start with Uncle Vernon going to work and encountering Wizards on
the streets. Don’t start with the Intergalactic Federation, start with Princess Leia running
away from Darth Vader to get a message to Obi Wan. Break your audience in gently or
they might spook. Think about this as a learning curb for the audience, the less steep the
curb, the easier it is for the audience to understand your world and therefore immerse
themselves in it. Note that the younger the audience the lower the curb should be.
If you’ve successfully laid the simple character-driven ground work that allows the

themselves in it. Note that the younger the audience the lower the curb should be.
If you’ve successfully laid the simple character-driven ground work that allows the
audience to suspend their disbelief and accept the characters exist in your world, then they
will accept the more complicated details. Once you’ve established and grounded your
world, characters and audience, you can then start hanging the bells and whistles on your
world: showing the details, but do not feel the need to rush it. Do not overwhelm the
audience with too much lore immediately. Allow them to gradually discover it as your
protagonist progresses on their journey. Start simple.
Show Don’t Tell:
It is important to avoid exposition, but if you are finding it hard to get the finer details of
your world across to the audience, Apprentice Plots are a useful tool to break the audience
in. See your world through the eyes of a newbie who is learning about the world in tandem

your world across to the audience, Apprentice Plots are a useful tool to break the audience
in. See your world through the eyes of a newbie who is learning about the world in tandem
with the audience, like Doctor Watson in the Sherlock Holmes Stories, Holmes can reel off
exposition to the audience by reeling it off to Watson. Be cautious that this is somewhat of
a cheat code and has been done to death. The easiest way of showing instead of telling is
to make sure your characters actively interact with the world around them.
(Note: Peter Jackson’s Fellowship of the Ring prologue and Star War’s opening crawl is
cheating! Try and avoid resorting to these stylised exposition dumps and only use them if
strictly necessary to flesh out the history of your world!)
7

You’re a Wizard, Harry!
Let’s talk about magic! I know that not every story will contain magic, but the lessons you
can learn from how to handle magic, and how to build magic systems in your world
building are useful in learning how to handle setting, plot and character.
Hard and Soft Magic:
Firstly, let’s talk about the different types of magic available to you. There is a wide
spectrum of magic. Sanderson breaks this down into soft magic at one end of the
spectrum, and hard magic at the other. Of course your magic can fall anywhere in
between, but understanding the two extremes is important in creating a logical and
believable magic system.
Hard Magic:
Hard magic adheres to strict, well-defined rules. It is more of a science. It's all about
creating a system with clear cause-and-effect relationships, where characters and the
audience understand the mechanics of spells, their abilities and limitations.
Soft Magic:

creating a system with clear cause-and-effect relationships, where characters and the
audience understand the mechanics of spells, their abilities and limitations.
Soft Magic:
Soft magic is less well defined. The rules are more flexible, and characters and the
audience might not fully understand how it works. To sum it up in a word, soft magic is
about Wonder. Soft magic is often used in a symbolic and metaphorical manner.
Examples:
The world of Harry Potter largely consists of hard magic, well-defined spells with rules,
allowing the characters and audience to learn about and understand the magical system.
However, the most powerful magic force is love. Love is a thematic soft magic that imbues
the stories with a sense of wonder.
In Lord of the Rings, magic is largely a soft force. It lacks rigid rules, leaving room for
wonder. Although the audience believes that Gandalf may have hard magical abilities,

In Lord of the Rings, magic is largely a soft force. It lacks rigid rules, leaving room for
wonder. Although the audience believes that Gandalf may have hard magical abilities,
these abilities are never explained, often happening in the background, keeping them in
the realms of soft magic. However, some elements are made from harder magic, like the
One Ring with its explicit rules: if you wear it you turn invisible, but at the cost of Sauron
being able to see you and it corrupting your mind.
These stories both demonstrate perfect examples of the potential in balancing between
soft and hard magic. Allowing your audience to both understand the magic, and therefore
intellectually participating with it, whilst simultaneously not losing their sense of wonder.
Sanderson’s Laws:
Brandon Sanderson came up with three laws to consider when developing magic systems
in world building:
Sanderson's First Law:
“An author's ability to solve conflict with magic is directly proportional to how well the

in world building:
Sanderson's First Law:
“An author's ability to solve conflict with magic is directly proportional to how well the
reader understands said magic. “
Magic isn't just a get-out-of-jail-free card. It is important your magic system has clear and
consistent rules. It is important to earn the right to use your magic. It needs to be properly
foreshadowed, with a clear set up and pay off. Your magic should have limitations and a
8

well-defined structure so the audience can follow how it works, helping you avoid any
moments of deus ex machina.
But what if you’re not writing about magic? These rules still apply. They can be conflated
with with the setting and the characters.
Just like with magic, the more your audience understands about your world, the better they
can connect with it. If you're writing about a time or a place, make sure your readers know
its rules and how it operates. With your characters make sure their arcs are properly set up
and developed, make sure their motivations are well established and their subsequent
actions are clear.
Sanderson's Second Law:
“Limitations > Powers.”
It's not all about what magic can do; it's about what it can't do. Limitations are where the
real magic happens! Restrictions and rules make the story more interesting. It's where the
challenges and conflicts are. It’s like two cowboys in a shootout, it’s not the guns that adds

real magic happens! Restrictions and rules make the story more interesting. It's where the
challenges and conflicts are. It’s like two cowboys in a shootout, it’s not the guns that adds
the drama; its the number of bullets they have.
The idea of limitation being greater or more important than the power can be used in
developing your setting. If you write about a sun drenched world where everything runs on
solar power, it’s what happens when the clouds roll in and the sun disappears that you will
find your drama.
When it comes to character, their flaws, vulnerabilities, and personal struggles make them
more compelling. It's the limitations that make them real and relatable.
This can be broken down into flaws, limitations and cost. Flaws is what your character can
not currently do; they will have to work and train to overcome these flaws. Limitations is
what the character can not do; a permanent limitation that they have to learn to live and

not currently do; they will have to work and train to overcome these flaws. Limitations is
what the character can not do; a permanent limitation that they have to learn to live and
work with. Cost is what your character has to give up in order to get what they want. Harry
Potter has to give up his life to defeat Voldemort. Peter Parker has to risk his normal life to
become Spiderman.
Sanderson's Third Law:
“Expand what you already have before you add something new.”
Before you go adding a bunch of new stuff to your magical system, explore what you've
already got and expand on what's already there. This keeps things consistent and avoids
making your magic system look like a jumbled mess. More is not strictly better. It is easier
to get submerged in a deep well than it is in an inch deep ocean.
When it comes to characters, delve into their backgrounds, motivations, and relationships
before throwing new characters into the mix. It makes the story richer and keeps

When it comes to characters, delve into their backgrounds, motivations, and relationships
before throwing new characters into the mix. It makes the story richer and keeps
everything consistent and engaging.
In world building, it's about making your setting more immersive. A well developed village
is more interesting than a hundred under developed cities.
Sanderson’ Zeroth Law:
Sanderson also has a fourth rule referred to as Sanderson’ Zeroth Law:
He simply states, “always air on the side of what is awesome!”
The expression, ‘the world is at your finger tips’ doesn’t do it justice. Every conceivable
universe is at your finger tips! You can write anything, create anything, say anything! Don’t
hold back and just be awesome!
9

The Beginning of Wisdom
With this myriad of infinite possibilities stretched out before you, it can get a bit
overwhelming, not just for you, but for the audience too. The simplest way to balance
these possibilities within a world that feels consistent and believable is to constantly come
back to the word ‘Logic’.
There’s two types of logic you need to think about:
Internal logic and external logic.
Internal Logic:
Think of internal logic as setting up the ground rules for your world. It's the framework that
defines how everything functions, from the structure of your societies and the laws of
nature, to how magic and technology works. The key is that these rules should make
sense within the context of your world, and they should stay consistent unless there's a
very good reason for change, but even this change should make logical sense within your
world. Gravity can suddenly disappear but you still need to the audience to understand
why.

very good reason for change, but even this change should make logical sense within your
world. Gravity can suddenly disappear but you still need to the audience to understand
why.
If your world's rules change without rhyme or reason, the audience can become
disoriented and lose the thread of the story. Consistency is key for keeping your audience
immersed and satisfied. Immersion is about emotional engagement. When your world's
internal logic is well established and understood, it can intensify the emotional impact of
your story.
When your internal logic and rules are consistent and the audience understand these
rules, they can predict how they might effect the story. They become active participants in
your world. Predictability isn't necessarily a bad thing. Audiences can feel cheated if a
story goes to far from their expectations.
If the murderer turns out to be a random character you have introduced in the third act, the

story goes to far from their expectations.
If the murderer turns out to be a random character you have introduced in the third act, the
audience will feel like they have wasted their time. When your audience knows how your
world operates, they can anticipate what might happen next. This anticipation increases
their connection with the characters and keeps them more immersed in the story.
(For longer series, it's beneficial to introduce slight gaps in your internal logic. Suppose
you have a wizard who knows all magic, and later you need a new spell to resolve a plot
point. If the wizard conveniently performs this new magic without explanation, the
audience might feel shortchanged. By establishing that the wizard doesn't know
everything, you allow room for character growth and new additions. While in a standalone
story, you could backtrack in the edit and foreshadow the new magic, in a series, you're
bound by the world you've already created and delivered to your audience.)

story, you could backtrack in the edit and foreshadow the new magic, in a series, you're
bound by the world you've already created and delivered to your audience.)
In your world, just like in reality, actions should have consequences. If your characters
breaks the rules, there must be repercussions. The choices and decisions made by
characters should lead to evolution. These outcomes, whether positive or negative, will
impact character growth and progress the story.
If the audience know that certain actions will lead to certain outcomes it will increase the
overall tension. If you established the laws and a character breaks them, they might go to
jail. If you've established the necessity of oxygen and a character's space suit
malfunctions, they won’t be able to breath.
Every conflict in your story should be built on cause and effect, anchoring conflicts in the
logic of your world. This ensures that conflicts are grounded in the logic of your world. As a

Every conflict in your story should be built on cause and effect, anchoring conflicts in the
logic of your world. This ensures that conflicts are grounded in the logic of your world. As a
result, when characters resolve conflicts, the outcomes feel earned and satisfying and the
10

audience will be a able to follow and empathise with your characters’ emotional arcs. This
consistent logic keeps the tension raised and the audience engaged.
Consistency helps facilitate the suspension of disbelief; a vital aspect of storytelling. When
your world's internal logic remains steady, it allows readers or viewers to immerse
themselves more deeply in the narrative without constantly questioning its plausibility.
Consistency also adds to the sense of realism. Even if your rules are different from the
rules of our reality, that constant consistency of your internal logic will help ground the
audience. Inconsistent world building can lead to plot holes that can confuse or frustrate
you and your audience. Consistency prevents such issues, helping maintain the structure
of your narrative.
External Logic:
External logic is the logic of our reality. Walls are solid, fires burn and cows go moo!
Consider how easy it is for your audience to step into your world. If your world is too

External Logic:
External logic is the logic of our reality. Walls are solid, fires burn and cows go moo!
Consider how easy it is for your audience to step into your world. If your world is too
convoluted or bizarre, you might put your audience off straight away. That’s not to say you
should not be bizarre, but take into account the learning curb of your audience and break
them in gently.
If everyone in your world walks backwards and never seem to bump into anything, even if
you have worked hard to establish the cultural reasons for them walking backwards, the
audience will not be able to accept the lack of bumping into things! If however the wealthy
walk backwards and they use servants to guide them, then the internal and external logic
work in tandem and the audience will accept this unusual quirk of your world. The key is to
strike that balance between uniqueness and familiarity. You want to captivate your
audience and not alienate them.

strike that balance between uniqueness and familiarity. You want to captivate your
audience and not alienate them.
External logic often involves using familiar elements, whether that is gravity, mothers
giving birth or cows going moo! You can draw inspiration from real-world cultures, history,
and landscapes to create unique and believable fictional worlds. It can help the audience
feel enough recognition that they do not feel immediately lost.
You can also use genre troupes to help maintain this sense of familiarity, as well as being
inspired by other works. Zombies have entered into the realms of external logic. Audiences
recognise Zombies, meaning you have to do less work to establish and explain them.
If you use enough external logic, and are aware of that external logic, then it also gives
you the opportunity to surprise the audience. As long as it makes sense in your internal
logic, you can use their preexisting expectations to subvert their exceptions and give the
story impact.

you the opportunity to surprise the audience. As long as it makes sense in your internal
logic, you can use their preexisting expectations to subvert their exceptions and give the
story impact.
Logic, whether internal or external, is your anchor and compass, guiding you and your
audience through your world, making it believable and relatable. Consistency is the
cornerstone of logic in world building. It brings believability, engagement, and depth to your
creation, building a reliable framework that both you and your audience can rely on. It
ensures that your story remains coherent and compelling, allowing the audience to fully
immerse themselves in your world.

A Brave New World
Okay, now it’s time for the fun part! What are the various elements that go into building a
world?
You can break these elements into two main categories:
The Physical Setting and the Cultural Setting (although several of these cross over as
culturally significant physical settings ie… cities, farms and magic).
(Remember to not feel intimidated by these lists. You do not need to include every
element. The only elements you need to include are those that your characters interact
with and only to the level of detail necessary to tell your story.)
Physical Setting:
Rules of physics:
What are the fundamental laws that make up the foundations your world's mechanics?
• These rules govern the behaviour of natural laws, such as how objects move and energy
flows, as well as how technology functions.
• These rules are what ensure that your world maintains a coherent internal logic.
In a world where people can manipulate gravity at will, cities may be built in the sky or on

• These rules are what ensure that your world maintains a coherent internal logic.
In a world where people can manipulate gravity at will, cities may be built in the sky or on
the sides of cliffs.
Weather, climate, and seasons:
Is your world hot, cold or something in between?
• These elements don't just determine if your characters need to wear sunscreen or not;
they mould the very landscapes and ecosystems of your world.
• They influence everything from agriculture to attire, as well as setting the tone for each
scene in your story.
In a world where unending storms ravage the land, and the sun only breaks through the
perpetual clouds for a few minutes each year. This unrelenting climate can shape your
landscapes with windswept deserts and subterranean cities, and give you characters a
clear obstacle to overcome in pursuit of their goals.
Maps:
Do you understand the layout of your world?
• Maps offer a visual guide to your world's layout, ensuring that the audience can navigate

clear obstacle to overcome in pursuit of their goals.
Maps:
Do you understand the layout of your world?
• Maps offer a visual guide to your world's layout, ensuring that the audience can navigate
your creation with clarity.
• Even if not shared with the audience, maps can still be useful to create for your own
sense of your world’s time and geography whilst writing.
• A map can also be useful MacGuffin (a plot device that pushes the story forward and
12

gets characters moving) helping set clear goals, and driving the plot forward.
When a farmhand finds an ancient map marked with an X he steals his boss’s horse and
goes in search of whatever treasures lie in wait.
Mountains, Valleys, Plains and Deserts:
What is the topography of your world?
• More than just a scenic backdrop, mountains, valleys, plains and deserts shape the very
identity of your world.
• They form natural barriers, dictate climate patterns, and influence the availability of
resources.
• These landscapes can offer clear, tangible goals and obstacles to your characters.
Climbing a mountain is a perfect example of story structure. A character has a clear goal:
to get to the top, obstacles: the mountain, its glaziers and ravines, and a resolution: to get
back down. A diagram of story structure looks like a mountain for a reason!
Tectonic activity:
What sculpted your continents, mountains, and oceans?
• Tectonic activity is the force shaping your landscapes and ecosystems.

Tectonic activity:
What sculpted your continents, mountains, and oceans?
• Tectonic activity is the force shaping your landscapes and ecosystems.
• Volcanoes are visually appealing and their natural volatility can be thematically
interesting.
In a world where tectonic activity is so intense that the continents move aggressively,
causing landmasses to collide and drift apart in a matter of years. This geological chaos
could create a nomadic lifestyle where cities are built on colossal mobile platforms, and
conflict arises through the uncontrolled movement of the cities.
Oceans, seas, lakes, and rivers:
What is the lifeblood of your world?
• Oceans, seas, lakes, and rivers aren't just bodies of water; they shape the very essence
of geography, climate, and ecosystems.
• They're the basis of trade routes, cultural influences, and resource distribution.
• They serve as natural barriers, focal points for conflict, and are vital avenues of
transportation.

• They're the basis of trade routes, cultural influences, and resource distribution.
• They serve as natural barriers, focal points for conflict, and are vital avenues of
transportation.
• Bodies of water are where you would find most cities, towns and villages.
In a world where there is nothing but ocean and the natural resources are all collected by
one giant wave constantly circumnavigating the planet. Civilisations would have to build
cities that follow behind the wave, with characters risking their lives to mine the stormy
depths of the tsunami.
Flora:
What colours your landscape?
13

• Plant life influences the diet, medicine, and materials available to your characters, having
a large impact on daily life.
• The location and variety of different plant species can effect different cultures, belief
systems, and traditions.
In a land where enormous, carnivorous plants dominate the landscape, humans might
have to build cites high above them, or deep below them, but if these dangerous plants
have a flower that contains the only medicine that can save the Queen’s life, the
characters would have to venture from the safety of their cities to save their Queen.
Fauna:
What non-sapiens share your world?
• Incorporating diverse fauna adds greatly to the complexity of your world.
• Whether a mighty dragon or a humble cow, they're not just part of the background; they
can impact agriculture, transportation, and the mythologies of your world.
• These creatures can be key players in the ecosystem of your world.
• They can be predators and pray.

• These creatures can be key players in the ecosystem of your world.
• They can be predators and pray.
• Diverse fauna will not only enrich your world, but present a variety of potential
challenges and opportunities to your characters.
In a world where enormous, flying birds fill the skies, cities are built on their backs, and
entire societies are centred around their migrations and behaviours.
Natural Resources:
What are the foundations of opportunity and wealth in your world?
• Natural resources determine the availability of essential materials and energy, affecting
technological advancements, trade networks, and societal structures.
• Settlements will be built up near resource rich areas, such as mines, forests, and water
sources.
In a world where there are only two mines containing the only metal that can be used to
make the space suits needed to survive, and one of those mines begins to run out of its

sources.
In a world where there are only two mines containing the only metal that can be used to
make the space suits needed to survive, and one of those mines begins to run out of its
supplies, the opposing forces will do anything to maintain control of the one remaining
mine.
Cosmology:
What effect do stars have on your world and story?
• Cosmology can shape the beliefs, rituals, calendars, and potentially the supernatural
elements of your world.
• They can also act as maps and compasses for your characters to navigate the world.
In a world where stars are sentient beings, with different societies worshipping different
stars, when one star is destroyed by another in battle, the faction worshipping the defeated

The essence of building a world, as reiterated time and again, is character. A rich,
immersive world sets the stage, but it is the characters, with their stories, desires, and
motivations, who breathe life into your world.
The spectrum of world building is vast, ranging from entirely unfamiliar realms like Middle
Earth to the streets of our own world. Regardless of the type of world you’re constructing,
its foundation is character, your story's genre and your target audience. Knowing this will
give you the clarity to ensure you build with purpose.
It's clear that the tip of the iceberg, or the surface level of your world, needs depth
beneath. But this depth doesn't need to be exhaustive; it merely needs to be convincing.

Two Kinds of Polytheism
It’s worth distinguishing between two different types of polytheism. The first is
henotheism, in which worshipers choose one god from a pantheon and focus their

different times as the situation demands. A farmer might pray to the lord of sun and
rain when his crop is growing and to the harvest mother when the crop is ready, but

in RPGs, even though it has been more prevalent in history.

How to Design a Mystery Cult
Adding a mystery cult or two to a campaign is a good way to add variety to those
anonymous high priests, blank temple facades, and stereotypical holy days. On top of
that, they can be a great source for adventure. After all, nothing gets the pot boiling
like a little mystery.

four simple questions should provide more than enough ideas for multiple adventures.

Open, Nested, and Secret Societies
Craft guilds and thieves’ guilds, knightly and priestly orders, mage’s colleges,
cults, aristocratic clubs, and secret societies: they are all organizations devoted
to some form of group action and purpose. But they are not structured the same
way when facing the public. The craft guilds keep their methods secret and the
wizards hide their arcane lore. The knights might have an open face to the world,
but hide their martial techniques and their battlefield commands, banner codes,
or special maneuvers and training methods. Priesthoods are known both for a
public face and their inner knowledge (see Zeb Cook’s essay on Mystery Cults for
more on this practice of the ancient world). And cults and secrets societies are
certainly secretive in what they do and do not reveal to others, especially if their
goals are malevolent.

Conclusion
Worldbuilding can be an enjoyable hobby for its own sake, and many game
designers still treat it as a way to explore various social or narrative issues in dozens
of environments and cultures, spinning out ever-greater quantities of material
for an existing setting. My own view is that this can be enjoyable but is ultimately
self-defeating, as the best worlds are memorable without requiring a 12-volume
set for beginners. Kitchen sink design, then, feeds fan desires in an unhealthy way,
and ultimately abdicates the primary function of game design—to make choices
that focus the game experience—by emphasizing all choices equally and providing
narrative and playspace for both popular and niche interests.
